definition_context.definition: p=(1/3)mn overline(v^2). Original n32 calls the mean square overline(v^2) the 均方速度. It is not the square root of that quantity.

facts: 1 to 1' is expansion at constant p1 in hot water until temperature T2.
1' to 2 is slow isothermal compression at temperature T2.

solutions.asked: Compare hydrogen and nitrogen molecular motion in the atmosphere.
solutions.independent_solution: For equilibrium gases at the same absolute temperature, (1/2)m overline(v^2)=(3/2)kT. H2 has molecular mass about 2 u versus N2 about 28 u, so overline(v_H2^2)/overline(v_N2^2)=14 and their rms-speed ratio is sqrt(14)=3.741657. Hydrogen molecules move faster in the characteristic thermal-speed sense.
solutions.units_models_conventions: Common local thermal-equilibrium temperature, molecular H2 and N2, not individual instantaneous speeds; no claim that every H2 molecule outruns every N2 molecule.

solutions.asked: Internal-energy changes in both directed paths of Figure 24 and all three directed paths of Figure 30.
solutions.independent_solution: A fixed amount of ideal gas has U depending only on absolute temperature. Figure 24: 1 to 1' has constant p1 and increasing V, so T=p1 V/(nR) increases and U increases. Original n17 explicitly defines 1' to 2 as isothermal compression at T2: U is unchanged, even though p increases and V decreases. Figure 30 is a V versus T diagram, not a p versus V diagram. 1 to 2 moves right along a line whose extension passes through the origin: T rises and U rises (V/T constant, isobaric). 2 to 3 moves vertically downward at fixed T: U unchanged. 3 to 1 moves left at fixed V: T and U fall. Ordered results: increase, unchanged; increase, unchanged, decrease.
solutions.units_models_conventions: No numerical temperature ratios or energy changes can be extracted from schematic pixel lengths. The original prose supplies the isothermal definition. Neither the modern path curvature nor a pixel product pV is a calibrated measurement.

solutions.asked: Compare molecular counts in 50 m^3 room air and 200 cm^3 liquid water at standard atmospheric pressure and 20 C.
solutions.independent_solution: For room air, N_air=pV/(kT), using p=101325 Pa, V=50 m^3 and T=293.15 K, gives 1.251738e27 molecules. Water is liquid, so use density approximately 1000 kg/m^3, V=200 cm^3=2e-4 m^3, mass approximately 0.2 kg and water molar mass approximately 0.018 kg/mol: N_water=(0.2/0.018) N_A=6.691268e24. N_air/N_water approximately 187.07. The room contains far more molecules despite liquid water having greater molecular number density.
solutions.units_models_conventions: Air modeled as an ideal gas; ordinary liquid-water density and molar mass approximations explicitly stated, not equal gas laws for both phases. At actual 20 C density near 998 kg/m^3 the ratio remains about 187 and the comparison is unchanged.

solutions.asked: Percentage increase of the source-defined mean-square molecular velocity of blood water from 37 C to 40 C.
solutions.independent_solution: Under the source kinetic-temperature model for unchanged molecular mass, overline(v^2) is proportional to absolute T. T1=310.15 K, T2=313.15 K, so percentage increase=100(T2/T1-1)=100*3/310.15=0.9672739 percent (using textbook 273 K offset: 0.9677419 percent), about 0.97 percent. This is not the rms-speed increase: sqrt(313.15/310.15)-1 gives 0.482473 percent, which answers a different quantity.
solutions.units_models_conventions: Faithfully uses original n32 overline(v^2), not a silently substituted modern rms convention. The equilibrium translational kinetic-temperature assumption is a model; the gas-pressure equation is not applied to liquid blood. No Celsius temperature ratio 40/37.

solutions.asked: Gas molecular count in 1 cm^3 at 1.3e-10 N/m^2 and 27 C.
solutions.independent_solution: N=pV/(kT). Convert 1 cm^3=1e-6 m^3 and 27 C=300.15 K. Then N=(1.3e-10*1e-6)/(1.380649e-23*300.15)=31370.52, approximately 3.14e4 molecules. Textbook T=300 K gives approximately 3.14e4. Use the stated SI pressure; 1e-12 mmHg is approximate (about 1.333e-10 Pa), not a new exact datum.
solutions.units_models_conventions: Ideal residual gas, p in Pa, SI volume, Boltzmann constant; no multiplication by N_A after computing molecule count.

solutions.asked: Temperature rise of 4 mol monoatomic ideal gas during an adiabatic compressor stroke with 500 J work.
solutions.independent_solution: Compression means external work on the gas, W_on=+500 J (equivalently work by the gas W_by=-500 J). Adiabatic Q=0 and first law Delta U=Q+W_on=500 J. Monoatomic ideal gas U=(3/2)nRT, so Delta T=500/((3/2)*4*R)=10.02270 K with R=8.314462618 J/(mol K), approximately 10 K, also a 10 C temperature difference.
solutions.units_models_conventions: Fixed 4 mol, closed monoatomic ideal-gas system with no other energy reservoirs in the textbook model. A reading of +500 J as work by the gas would yield cooling, contradicting the stated compression; the work sign is explicit rather than silently assumed.

sourceLimits: Molecular speed comparison is statistical at a common temperature, not a universal ordering of individual molecules.
Mean-square velocity and rms speed are distinct; original n32 controls Q4.
Figures are schematic and supply no calibrated numerical products or temperatures.
Liquid-water molecular counts require an approximate material density; ideal-gas modeling cannot be extended to the water cup.
Compression work is positive on the gas and negative by the gas.
